  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Vignette:
The event that changed everything for Harold happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late October, during what should have been an uneventful shift at a downtown government office building. He was seventy-one years old, a security guard for nearly a decade, and his job had always been about routine: checking badges, scanning packages, nodding at the same faces day after day. That afternoon, a man in a long coat walked past the metal detector without stopping. Harold called out, stood up from his desk, and then there was the noise—a sound he still could not order into a coherent sequence no matter how many times he tried. He remembered glass, remembered shouting, remembered the weight of his own body hitting the floor, but the middle of it, the part where the assailant swung a metal pipe and connected with Harold’s shoulder and ribs, existed only as a smear of sensation without narrative. He could not tell the story to himself in any way that made sense. What he could recall, with excruciating clarity, were details that had no business being so vivid: the pattern of the man’s jacket buttons, the smell of burnt coffee from the lobby machine, the exact angle of light falling across the tile floor as he lay there waiting for help.

In the weeks that followed, Harold found himself unable to stop turning the event over in his mind, but the turning was not toward understanding. It was toward revenge. He spent hours imagining what he would do if he ever saw the man again, how he would get even, how he would make sure the man felt every bit of the humiliation and pain Harold now carried. These thoughts arrived without invitation and stayed for entire afternoons, leaving him exhausted and no less angry. At the same time, something strange happened when he tried to revisit the actual moment of the attack: he felt nothing. Sometimes he could recall what happened and feel completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger, as if the man on the floor was someone else entirely. This absence of feeling disturbed him more than the anger did, because it made him wonder whether he had lost something essential, whether he had already become a person who could not feel his own life.

He had come to believe that he could not cope with even the slightest upset now. A loud noise in a parking lot sent his heart racing for an hour. An unexpected knock at the door made him freeze mid-step. He was certain that somebody else—a younger guard, a tougher man, anyone—would not have gotten into this situation in the first place. They would have seen it coming, would have reacted faster, would not have ended up on the floor like a fool. The worst appraisal, the one that sat heaviest in his chest, was the conviction that he had failed in his most important role in life. He was supposed to protect people. That was what a security guard did, what a husband did, what a man his age with decades of experience should be able to do without thinking. Instead, he had become someone who needed protection, and that failure felt permanent.

Harold’s wife noticed the changes before he did. He stopped going to the grocery store with her because the aisles felt too narrow and the people too close. At home, he always sat with his back against the wall, positioning his chair so he could see the entire room, including the doorway. He told her it was just a habit, but he knew it was more than that: he was watching for dangerous people, scanning every face that entered a room, cataloging threats that no one else seemed to see. His job became impossible. He could not stand at the front desk anymore without his eyes darting to every approaching figure, without his hands trembling as he reached for a badge. He took medical leave, then early retirement. The days stretched out in front of him, empty and loud with vigilance.

What finally brought Harold to seek help was not the fear or the anger or the numbness, but the silence. His wife had stopped asking him how he was doing. She moved around him carefully, as though he were something fragile that might shatter if touched. He saw the worry in her face and understood that he was no longer the man she had married, that he had become a problem she had to manage. He came to the clinic because he was afraid of losing her, and because he was even more afraid that he had already lost himself. He hoped, though he could not say it out loud, that someone might help him find a way back to the person who used to sit at a desk and greet people with a nod, before the glass broke and the light fell wrong and he became a stranger to his own story.
